subtopic: Dynamic warm-up and joint mobility drills for runners

claims.claim: A structured warm-up that includes activity beyond stretching improves subsequent physical performance in the large majority of measured outcomes.
claims.evidence: Systematic review and meta-analysis of 32 high-quality studies found that warm-up improved performance in 79% of the criteria examined, with little evidence that warming up is detrimental. Because most included studies were not randomized controlled trials, the authors called for more RCTs.

citation.title: Effects of warming-up on physical performance: a systematic review with meta-analysis
citation.authors: Fradkin AJ, Zazryn TR, Smoliga JM
citation.venue: Journal of Strength and Conditioning Research

claims.claim: Dynamic stretching in the warm-up improves sprint and jump performance, while static stretching can reduce it.
claims.evidence: Network meta-analysis of lower-limb explosive strength found dynamic stretching significantly improved countermovement jump height (MD 1.60 cm, 95% CI 0.67 to 2.60) and sprint time (MD -0.08 s), while static stretching showed a small significant negative effect on sprint time (MD 0.07 s).

citation.title: A systematic review and net meta-analysis of the effects of different warm-up methods on the acute effects of lower limb explosive strength
citation.authors: Multiple authors (BMC Sports Science, Medicine and Rehabilitation)
citation.venue: BMC Sports Science, Medicine and Rehabilitation (PMC10463540)

claims.claim: For explosive performance, roughly 7 to 10 minutes of dynamic stretching in the warm-up gave the largest benefit.
claims.evidence: The net meta-analysis reported that dynamic stretching improved jump and sprint outcomes, and the effect was moderated by stretching duration, with the strongest effect size at 7 to 10 minutes.

citation.title: A systematic review and net meta-analysis of the effects of different warm-up methods on the acute effects of lower limb explosive strength
citation.authors: Multiple authors (BMC Sports Science, Medicine and Rehabilitation)
citation.venue: BMC Sports Science, Medicine and Rehabilitation (PMC10463540)

claims.claim: Putting dynamic stretching rather than static stretching in the warm-up improves both lower-limb performance and range of motion.
claims.evidence: Systematic review with meta-analysis in physically active people concluded that dynamic stretching in the warm-up has greater positive effects on lower-limb performance and range of motion than static stretching, and recommends dynamic stretching for sports needing lower-extremity performance.

citation.title: Does the Inclusion of Static or Dynamic Stretching in the Warm-Up Routine Improve Jump Height and ROM in Physically Active Individuals? A Systematic Review with Meta-Analysis
citation.authors: Multiple authors (Applied Sciences)

claims.claim: Prolonged static stretching on its own, especially holds longer than about 60 seconds, can transiently reduce maximal strength and power.
claims.evidence: Narrative review of acute effects of static and dynamic stretching reported that static stretches of sufficient duration can impair subsequent force and power output. This is why static holds are moved to after training or after the warm-up.

citation.title: A review of the acute effects of static and dynamic stretching on performance
citation.authors: Behm DG, Chaouachi A

claims.topic: Static stretching within a full warm-up
claims.claim: Short static stretches added inside an otherwise complete dynamic warm-up do not harm performance.
claims.evidence: A controlled trial found no effect of muscle stretching within a full dynamic warm-up on athletic performance, which shows the negative static-stretching effect is driven by long isolated holds in an otherwise incomplete warm-up.

citation.title: No effect of muscle stretching within a full, dynamic warm-up on athletic performance
citation.authors: Blazevich AJ, Gill ND, Kvorning T, et al.
citation.venue: Medicine and Science in Sports and Exercise

claims.claim: The RAMP framework (Raise, Activate and Mobilise, Potentiate) is a widely used structure that sequences warm-up work: raise body temperature, activate and mobilise key joints and muscles, then potentiate with fast or sport-specific work.
claims.evidence: RAMP was developed by strength and conditioning coach Ian Jeffreys and is described across coaching and peer-reviewed sources as a structured four-phase warm-up. A 2025 randomized crossover trial describes the phases as Raise (low-intensity aerobic work), Activate (dynamic drills such as lunges and leg swings), Mobilize (hurdle steps, lateral shuffles), and Potentiate (sprints and jumps).

citation.title: Acute effects of the RAMP warm-up on sprint and jump performance in youth soccer players
citation.authors: Girginer FG, et al.

claims.claim: A RAMP-structured warm-up improved acute sprint and jump performance compared with no warm-up and compared with static stretching.
claims.evidence: Randomized controlled crossover trial in 14 youth soccer players (aged 16 to 22) compared no warm-up, static stretching, and RAMP over three sessions. Sprint and jump performance were enhanced after the RAMP warm-up.

citation.title: Acute effects of the RAMP warm-up on sprint and jump performance in youth soccer players
citation.authors: Girginer FG, et al.

claims.claim: For trained runners racing 5000 m, a higher-intensity warm-up improved time trial performance by about 6.4 seconds (0.5%) versus a low-intensity warm-up.
claims.evidence: Study in trained long-distance runners found continuous running near 17 km/h during warm-up (versus about 12 km/h) improved 5000 m time trial performance by 6.4 s (0.5%), with the benefit appearing in the opening splits.

citation.title: Effects of High-Intensity Warm-Up on 5000-Meter Performance Time in Trained Long-Distance Runners
citation.authors: Alves MDDJ, et al.
citation.venue: Journal of Sports Science and Medicine

claims.claim: A hard or fast warm-up only helps if it is followed by a recovery window of roughly 18 to 20 minutes before the race.
claims.evidence: The 5000 m study and related work noted that high-intensity warm-ups produced performance gains when a transition period of 18 to 20 minutes followed; without that recovery window, other studies found no improvement.

citation.title: Effects of High-Intensity Warm-Up on 5000-Meter Performance Time in Trained Long-Distance Runners
citation.authors: Alves MDDJ, et al.
citation.venue: Journal of Sports Science and Medicine

claims.claim: Warm-up intensity influences short-distance running performance even when recovery is prolonged.
claims.evidence: Paris et al. reported that warm-up intensity influenced running performance despite prolonged recovery, supporting the view that the pace of the warm-up matters, not just its presence.

citation.title: Warm up intensity influences running performance despite prolonged recovery
citation.authors: Paris HL, Sinai EC, Leist MA, Crain CM, Keller AM, Malysa W, Renzullo SC
citation.venue: International Journal of Sports Science and Coaching

claims.claim: For intermediate-distance running, a shorter warm-up produces less physiological strain and can support performance as well as a long one.
claims.evidence: van den Tillaar and colleagues compared short and long warm-ups and found that the shorter option caused less fatigue, which is relevant for runners who cannot afford to burn energy before a hard effort.

citation.title: Effects of short or long warm-up on intermediate running performance
citation.authors: van den Tillaar R, Vatten T, Von Heimburg E
citation.venue: Journal of Strength and Conditioning Research

claims.claim: Stretching before exercise does not reduce the risk of exercise-related injury.
claims.evidence: Evidence-based summary of six trials (N = 5,130) found stretching did not decrease lower-limb soft tissue injuries (relative risk 0.85, 95% CI 0.65 to 1.1). Stretching is therefore not a reliable injury-prevention tool on its own.

citation.title: Stretching for Prevention of Exercise-Related Injury
citation.authors: American Family Physician (summary of Cochrane evidence)

claims.claim: Stretching before or after exercise gives only a tiny, not clinically meaningful, reduction in muscle soreness.
claims.evidence: Cochrane review found pre-exercise stretching reduced soreness at one day by about half a point on a 100-point scale (mean difference -0.52, 95% CI -11.30 to 10.26), which is far below a meaningful change.

citation.title: Stretching to prevent or reduce muscle soreness after exercise
citation.authors: Herbert RD, de Noronha M, Kamper SJ

claims.claim: Routine static stretching does not reduce overall injury rates, and only preliminary evidence suggests it may reduce musculotendinous injuries.
claims.evidence: Systematic review of four randomized and three controlled trials concluded there was moderate to strong evidence that routine static stretching does not reduce overall injury rates. Three of the seven studies reported significant reductions in musculotendinous and ligament injuries, which the authors called only preliminary.

citation.title: A systematic review into the efficacy of static stretching as part of a warm-up for the prevention of exercise-related injury
citation.authors: Small K, Mc Naughton L, Matthews M

claims.claim: Ankle dorsiflexion range of motion is linked to running and landing mechanics, and a deficit is associated with several lower-limb injuries.
claims.evidence: A clinical decision-making review reports that restricted dorsiflexion can reduce force absorption and is a risk factor for lateral ankle sprain, chronic ankle instability, Achilles tendinopathy, metatarsal stress fracture, plantar heel pain, and patellar tendinopathy.

citation.title: Restoring ankle dorsiflexion range of motion in athletes: an individualized clinical decision-making system
citation.authors: Multiple authors (PMC12585996)
citation.venue: Frontiers in Sports and Active Living (PMC12585996)

claims.claim: Reduced ankle dorsiflexion mobility can lower sprinting and jumping ability.
claims.evidence: A 2024 study on the relationship between ankle dorsiflexion range of motion and performance concluded that reduced dorsiflexion mobility may affect sprinting and jumping ability in young athletes.

citation.title: Relationship between ankle dorsiflexion range of motion and sprinting, jumping and change of direction ability
citation.authors: Cerrillo-Sanchis J, et al.

claims.claim: People with patellofemoral pain show reduced gluteus medius activity when running, which supports hip and glute activation work for runners with knee pain.
claims.evidence: Systematic review of running-related gluteus medius function found the strongest evidence was a moderate and significant reduction in gluteus medius duration of activity when running in people with patellofemoral pain.

citation.title: Running related gluteus medius function in health and injury: A systematic review with meta-analysis
citation.authors: Semciw AI, Green RA, Murley GS, Pizzari T

claims.topic: Strength and plyometrics for running economy
claims.claim: Plyometric training and heavy strength training improve running economy in distance runners, which is why controlled jumps and skips belong in a runner's programme.
claims.evidence: Meta-analysis of strength training in middle- and long-distance runners found heavy load and combined methods produced small to moderate running economy improvements, and plyometric training improved running economy at speeds up to 12 km/h.

citation.title: Effect of Strength Training Programs in Middle- and Long-Distance Runners' Economy at Different Running Speeds: A Systematic Review with Meta-analysis
citation.authors: Multiple authors (Sports Medicine)

claims.claim: Heavy resistance training improves running economy in highly trained runners.
claims.evidence: Systematic review with meta-analysis of controlled trials found an overall large beneficial effect of strength training on running economy in highly trained middle- and long-distance runners.

citation.title: The effects of strength training on running economy in highly trained runners: a systematic review with meta-analysis of controlled trials
citation.authors: Balsalobre-Fernandez C, Santos-Concejero J, Grivas GV
citation.venue: Journal of Strength and Conditioning Research

claims.claim: A-skips and B-skips are only moderately related to short-sprint performance and do not by themselves drive faster sprinting, so they train rhythm and front-side mechanics rather than substituting for fast running.
claims.evidence: Study of 63 young male athletes found A-skip and B-skip had good inter-rater reliability but only moderate predictive validity for 5 m and 20 m sprint performance, with B-skip the strongest predictor (5 m: beta -0.531, p < 0.01; 20 m: beta -0.322, p < 0.05). The authors noted the drills' direct effectiveness in enhancing sprint speed and acceleration appears constrained, with their value lying in knee elevation and kinematics rather than speed gains.

citation.title: Development and Validation of a Running Drill Test Battery to Predict 5 m and 20 m Sprint Performance
citation.authors: Matijasevic P, Males J, Cikojevic L, Zuvela F, Kuvacic G

claims.claim: For most recreational runners a short warm-up is enough, and for easy and steady runs about 5 to 10 minutes fits common practice, scaling up with session intensity.
claims.evidence: Randomized crossover trial in 12 recreational distance runners found moderate-duration dynamic stretching within the warm-up (about 60 seconds per leg) improved running economy and running performance. No trial sets an exact 5 to 10 minute threshold, so that figure is coaching practice rather than a measured dose.

citation.title: Moderate-Duration Dynamic Stretching During Warm-up Improves Running Economy and Running Performance in Recreational Distance Runners
citation.authors: Panasci M, Ferrando V, Bisio A, Filipas L, Di Gennaro S, Puce L, Ruggeri P, Faelli E
citation.venue: International Journal of Sports Physiology and Performance

claims.claim: Dynamic stretching does not impair performance and can improve range of motion and power.
claims.evidence: Review of the current literature on acute dynamic stretching concluded it does not compromise performance and can improve muscle flexibility alongside power, unlike long static holds.

citation.title: Acute effects of dynamic stretching on muscle flexibility and performance: an analysis of the current literature
citation.authors: Opplert J, Babault N

claims.claim: Warm-up is widely used to prepare for activity, but its effect on injury risk specifically is not firmly established by the performance literature.
claims.evidence: The performance meta-analysis by Fradkin et al. focused on performance and noted the shortage of randomized controlled trials; injury-prevention claims are separate and, for stretching, are not supported.

citation.title: Effects of warming-up on physical performance: a systematic review with meta-analysis
citation.authors: Fradkin AJ, Zazryn TR, Smoliga JM
citation.venue: Journal of Strength and Conditioning Research

claims.claim: Strength training reduces the risk of acute and overuse sports injuries, while stretching does not reduce injury risk. This is the general case for including hip and glute strengthening in a runner's programme.
claims.evidence: Systematic review and meta-analysis of 25 randomized trials (N = 26,610, 3,464 injuries) found strength training reduced sports injuries to less than a third (RR 0.315, 95% CI 0.207 to 0.480) and overuse injuries by about half (RR 0.527, 95% CI 0.373 to 0.746), while stretching had no beneficial effect (RR 0.963, 95% CI 0.846 to 1.095).

citation.title: The effectiveness of exercise interventions to prevent sports injuries: a systematic review and meta-analysis of randomised controlled trials
citation.authors: Lauersen JB, Bertelsen DM, Andersen LB

claims.claim: In runners and jumpers with patellofemoral pain, a hip and core strengthening programme resolved pain about a week sooner and built more hip strength than a knee-focused programme, though both improved.
claims.evidence: Multicenter randomized controlled trial of 199 patients with patellofemoral pain over 6 weeks found both the hip and core and the knee protocols improved pain, function and strength, but the hip and core protocol reduced visual analog pain scores one week earlier and produced greater gains in hip-abductor and hip-extensor strength and posterior core endurance.

citation.title: Strengthening of the hip and core versus knee muscles for the treatment of patellofemoral pain: a multicenter randomized controlled trial
citation.authors: Ferber R, Bolgla L, Earl-Boehm JE, Emery C, Hamstra-Wright K

claims.claim: There is no single optimal warm-up duration; a short warm-up can be 5 minutes or less and a long one over 20 minutes, and the right length tracks the session demands and the athlete.
claims.evidence: International expert consensus (Delphi study, 23 experts across 12 countries, 3 voting rounds) did not identify an optimal warm-up duration. It agreed a short warm-up may last 5 minutes or less while a long one may exceed about 20 minutes, that many warm-ups run 15 to 20 minutes, and that exercise selection, sequencing and loading may matter more than duration alone.

citation.title: International Expert Consensus on Warm-Up Protocols for Athletes: A Delphi Study
citation.authors: Boullosa D, Gil-Calvo M, Xenofondos A, Patikas DA, Blazevich AJ, Afonso J, Loturco I, Behm D, Xu K, Babault N, et al.
citation.venue: International Journal of Sports Physiology and Performance

claims.claim: A single warm-up does not give immediate injury protection, but preventive strength and balance exercises done regularly may reduce longer-term injury risk.
claims.evidence: The international warm-up consensus did not support an immediate injury-protection effect from one warm-up, and only 3 of 8 health and injury statements reached the 80% agreement threshold. The experts agreed that regularly performed preventive strength and balance exercises, whether in the warm-up or elsewhere in training, may reduce longer-term injury risk.

citation.title: International Expert Consensus on Warm-Up Protocols for Athletes: A Delphi Study
citation.authors: Boullosa D, Gil-Calvo M, Xenofondos A, Patikas DA, Blazevich AJ, Afonso J, Loturco I, Behm D, Xu K, Babault N, et al.
citation.venue: International Journal of Sports Physiology and Performance

claims.claim: During A-skips, B-skips and heel flicks the foot and ankle work through less dorsiflexion and produce less midtarsal power than during distance running, so the drills rehearse front-side mechanics rather than copying running's ankle loading.
claims.evidence: Seventeen long-distance runners performed five running drills and a run at 3.88 m/s. The A-skip, B-skip and heel flicks produced smaller ankle, midtarsal and metatarsophalangeal dorsiflexion peaks than running (all p < 0.001), and the A-skip and B-skip produced less midtarsal positive power, while joint moments did not differ from running.

citation.title: A comparison of foot and ankle biomechanics during running drills and distance running
citation.authors: Abran G, Berraz A, Dardenne N, Gramage K, Bornheim S, Delvaux F, Croisier JL, Schwartz C

catalog_candidates.name: Leg swings (front to back)
catalog_candidates.why: Gets your hips moving through a useful range before you load them with running.
catalog_candidates.feel: Loose and light at the front and back of the hip, no pinching.
form: Hold a wall or post for balance
Swing one leg forward and back from the hip, not the knee
Keep the torso tall and the swing relaxed
mistakes: Forcing range with a jerky kick
Rounding the lower back as the leg swings
Letting the knee bend and straighten to create the swing

catalog_candidates.name: Hip circles
catalog_candidates.why: Takes the hip joint through a full smooth circle so it moves freely before running.
catalog_candidates.feel: A smooth loop of motion in the hip, no catch or pinch.
form: Stand tall on one leg or hold support
Lift the other knee and draw a slow circle with it
Keep the circle controlled and even
mistakes: Rushing the circle
Letting the standing knee collapse inward
Using the lower back to force the range

catalog_candidates.name: Walking hip openers
catalog_candidates.why: Wakes up the outside of the hip and groin while you travel forward.
catalog_candidates.feel: A stretch across the front hip and a turn in the hip socket.
form: Step forward, lift one knee to hip height
Turn the knee outward, then step down
Alternate sides as you walk
mistakes: Leaning back to lift the knee
Turning from the lower back instead of the hip
Dropping the foot heavily

catalog_candidates.name: Ankle rocks
catalog_candidates.why: Restores the forward knee-over-toe ankle range that running and landing need.
catalog_candidates.feel: A stretch low in the calf and front of the ankle.
form: Kneel on one knee with the front foot flat
Drive the front knee forward over the toes
Keep the heel down and the foot pointing straight ahead
mistakes: Letting the heel lift
Turning the foot outward
Bouncing the knee instead of a smooth rock

catalog_candidates.name: World's greatest stretch
catalog_candidates.why: One move that covers hip, hamstring and mid-back at once, before a hard session.
catalog_candidates.feel: A long line from calf to hip, plus a twist through the upper back.
form: Step into a deep lunge
Place both hands inside the front foot
Drop the back knee, then reach one hand to the sky and twist
mistakes: Letting the front knee cave inward
Twisting from the hips instead of the ribs
Rushing before a stable lunge is set

catalog_candidates.name: Lunge with rotation
catalog_candidates.why: Loads the hips in a stride-like position and adds the trunk rotation running needs.
catalog_candidates.feel: A stretch at the front of the trailing hip with a turn through the chest.
form: Step into a forward lunge
Keep the torso tall and the front shin vertical
Rotate the chest toward the front leg, then step through
mistakes: Letting the front knee drift past the toes and inward
Leaning the torso forward
Rotating the pelvis instead of the ribcage

catalog_candidates.name: Inchworm
catalog_candidates.why: Mobilises the whole back line and warms the core and shoulders for a run.
catalog_candidates.feel: A stretch down the back of the legs as the hands walk out.
form: Stand tall, hinge and place hands on the floor
Walk the hands out to a plank
Walk the feet toward the hands and stand
mistakes: Letting the hips sag in the plank
Bending the knees to hide a tight hamstring
Rushing the walk-out

catalog_candidates.name: Cat-cow
catalog_candidates.why: Gets the spine moving smoothly through flexion and extension before you run.
catalog_candidates.feel: A gentle wave along the back, no sharp pinch.
form: Start on all fours, hands under shoulders
Arch the back up, then let it sag with the chest open
Match the motion to slow breathing
mistakes: Moving only the lower back
Forcing the end range
Speeding up and losing the breath rhythm

catalog_candidates.name: Thoracic rotations (quadruped t-spine)
catalog_candidates.why: Frees the mid-back so the trunk can rotate with the arms during running.
catalog_candidates.feel: A twist through the upper back with the shoulder opening toward the ceiling.
form: On all fours, place one hand behind the head
Rotate the elbow down toward the other arm, then up to the sky
Keep the hips still
mistakes: Rotating from the hips
Letting the lower back arch
Pulling the neck instead of the elbow

catalog_candidates.name: Arm circles
catalog_candidates.why: Warms the shoulders for the arm swing and counter-rotation of running.
catalog_candidates.feel: Light work around the shoulder with a smooth circle.
form: Stand tall with arms out to the sides
Draw small fast circles, then bigger slower ones
Reverse the direction
mistakes: Shrugging the shoulders to the ears
Circling from the elbow instead of the shoulder
Going so big the ribs flare

catalog_candidates.name: Monster walks (banded)
catalog_candidates.why: Turns on the side hip muscles that keep the knee tracking well over thousands of steps.
catalog_candidates.feel: A burning ache on the outer hip as you hold the stance.
form: Loop a band above the knees or at the ankles
Sit into a quarter squat
Step forward and out, keeping tension on the band
mistakes: Letting the knees cave in
Standing up out of the squat between steps
Taking steps so short the band goes slack

catalog_candidates.name: Clamshells (banded)
catalog_candidates.why: Targets the outer hip that stops the knee from dropping inward when you run.
catalog_candidates.feel: A focused burn on the upper outer glute.
form: Lie on your side, knees bent, band above the knees
Keep the feet together and lift the top knee
Lower slowly under control
mistakes: Rolling the pelvis back to open the knee
Lifting the foot with the knee
Rushing and losing hip position

catalog_candidates.name: Lateral band walk
catalog_candidates.why: Loads the hip in the sideways direction that running and single-leg stance demand.
catalog_candidates.feel: A steady burn on the outside of the hip through the whole set.
form: Band above the knees, quarter squat
Step sideways, leading with one leg
Keep the feet pointing forward and the stance low
mistakes: Dragging the trailing foot with no control
Standing tall and losing glute tension
Turning the toes outward

catalog_candidates.name: Banded glute bridge
catalog_candidates.why: Wakes up the glutes that drive hip extension in every stride.
catalog_candidates.feel: Glutes doing the work, not the lower back or hamstrings.
form: Lie on your back, feet flat, band above the knees
Press through the heels and lift the hips
Push the knees gently out against the band, then lower
mistakes: Arching the lower back at the top
Pushing through the toes
Letting the knees drop inward

catalog_candidates.name: A-skips
catalog_candidates.why: Rehearses a quick, high knee drive and a snappy foot strike under the body.
catalog_candidates.feel: Light and bouncy, with a strong knee lift and quick ground contact.
form: Drive one knee to hip height
Let the lower leg drop and strike under the body
Stay tall with a fast rhythm, not big steps
mistakes: Reaching the foot out in front
Leaning back
Losing the rhythm and slowing to a march

catalog_candidates.name: B-skips
catalog_candidates.why: Adds a pawing lower-leg action that trains the leg to sweep back and down.
catalog_candidates.feel: A knee lift with the foot flicking out and pawing back down.
form: Lift the knee as in an A-skip
Extend the lower leg out, then sweep the foot down and back
Keep the torso tall and rhythm quick
mistakes: Landing with a locked knee
Letting the extended leg reach too far forward
Turning it into a kick

catalog_candidates.name: High knees
catalog_candidates.why: Raises knee drive and leg-turnover rate while warming the hips and calves.
catalog_candidates.feel: Fast and light, heart rate rising, feet barely touching the ground.
form: Drive the knees to about hip height
Stay on the balls of the feet
Keep the torso tall and the arms pumping
mistakes: Leaning back to get the knees up
Landing flat-footed and heavy
Going slowly and losing the quick rhythm

catalog_candidates.name: Butt kicks
catalog_candidates.why: Warms the hamstrings and calves and trains a quick heel recovery.
catalog_candidates.feel: A fast flick of the heel toward the glute with a light bounce.
form: Jog forward, flicking the heels up toward the glutes
Keep the knees pointing down, not forward
Stay tall and quick
mistakes: Losing the rhythm and slowing to a walk
Overstriding as the heels flick back
Leaning forward from the waist

catalog_candidates.name: Straight-leg runs
catalog_candidates.why: Trains a stiff, quick leg that teaches fast ground contact and hamstring control.
catalog_candidates.feel: Stiff legs, quick contacts, a light prance forward.
form: Keep the legs mostly straight
Bounce forward off the balls of the feet
Use a quick, short ground contact
mistakes: Bending the knees like normal running
Reaching the legs out in front
Landing on the heels

catalog_candidates.name: High-knee dribbles
catalog_candidates.why: A short, quick version of high knees that sharpens foot speed and timing.
catalog_candidates.feel: Very fast, tiny steps with the knees coming up quickly.
form: Take short, rapid steps in place or moving slowly
Lift each knee quickly and lightly
Stay tall and keep the feet springy
mistakes: Traveling too far and stretching the steps
Heavy, flat landings
Dropping the knee height as you speed up

catalog_candidates.name: Carioca
catalog_candidates.why: Warms the hips and groin in the sideways direction and improves coordination.
catalog_candidates.feel: A quick cross-and-open foot pattern with the hips turning freely.
form: Travel sideways, alternating a cross-in-front step and a step behind
Keep the arms moving with the legs
Stay light on the feet and rhythmic
mistakes: Getting tangled by going too slowly
Turning the shoulders away from the direction of travel
Letting the feet drag heavily

catalog_candidates.name: Ankling
catalog_candidates.why: Warms the ankles and calves and trains a stiff, springy push off the ground.
catalog_candidates.feel: A springy bounce from the ankles with the feet barely leaving the ground.
form: Move forward with quick, tiny bounces from the ankles
Keep the knees almost straight
Land and push off with a stiff, springy ankle
mistakes: Bouncing from the knees instead of the ankles
Going slow and heavy
Landing on the heels

summary_tier_a: A structured warm-up improves running performance, and the strongest evidence favours dynamic work: dynamic stretching and drills improve sprint, jump and range of motion while long static holds can blunt power. The RAMP framework (Raise, Activate and Mobilise, Potentiate) sequences this well, and short dynamic drills plus a few strides cover most runners in 5 to 10 minutes. Static stretching does not prevent injury, so it does not belong at the front of a run; hip, ankle and glute activation drills earn their place for mechanics and injury resilience.
unverified: Exact minute-by-minute warm-up dose for recreational runners is still not fixed by direct dose-finding trials. The closest evidence is an international expert consensus (Boullosa et al. 2026), which found no optimal duration but placed a short warm-up at 5 minutes or less and a long one above about 20 minutes, and a recreational-runner crossover trial (Panasci et al. 2024) that improved running economy and performance with about 60 seconds per leg of dynamic stretching. No trial sets a measured 5 to 10 minute threshold, so that figure remains coaching practice.

Whether specific band drills such as clamshells and monster walks prevent knee pain is not established by controlled trials. The nearest evidence is broader: strength training reduced sports injuries to under a third and overuse injuries by about half (Lauersen et al. 2014), and hip and core strengthening resolved patellofemoral pain sooner than knee-focused work (Ferber et al. 2015), but no trial isolated clamshells or monster walks as a knee-pain prevention measure in runners.

Optimal reps, sets or passes for each running drill (A-skips, carioca) is coaching practice, not a tested dose-response. The running drill validation study (Matijasevic et al. 2025) scored drill quality against sprint times rather than dose, and no trial was found mapping drill volume to sprint mechanics or injury outcomes.
notes: Claim set balances systematic reviews and meta-analyses (Fradkin 2010, Behm and Chaouachi 2011, Opplert and Babault 2018, the 2023 and 2024 stretching meta-analyses, Cochrane soreness review, strength and running economy meta-analyses) with RCTs on warm-up intensity (Alves 2023, Paris 2021, van den Tillaar 2017) and the RAMP trial (Girginer 2025). The RAMP framework itself is coaching literature (Jeffreys) validated indirectly by the 2025 trial. Catalog candidates cover the 22 requested drills in three groups: general mobility (leg swings, hip circles, walking hip openers, ankle rocks, world's greatest stretch, lunge with rotation, inchworm, cat-cow, thoracic rotations, arm circles), banded glute activation (monster walks, clamshells, lateral band walk, banded glute bridge), and running-specific drills (A-skips, B-skips, high knees, butt kicks, straight-leg runs, high-knee dribbles, carioca, ankling). Durations are draft defaults for an app catalog and should be tuned during implementation. Two lower-confidence coaching citations are flagged as such and are used only for drill mechanics and recreational dose, not for performance claims. No em dashes used.
